original_value: Graphene is a material of particular interest for the implementation of sensors, and the ultimate performance of devices based on such a material is often determined by its flicker noise properties. Indeed, graphene exhibits, with respect to the vast majority of ordinary semiconductors, a peculiar behavior of the flicker noise power spectral density as a function of the charge carrier density. While in most materials flicker noise obeys the empirical Hooge law, with a power spectral density inversely proportional to the number of free charge carriers, in bilayer, and sometimes monolayer, graphene a counterintuitive behavior, with a minimum of flicker noise at the charge neutrality point, has been observed. We present an explanation for this stark difference, exploiting a model in which we enforce both the mass action law and the neutrality condition on the charge fluctuations deriving from trapping/detrapping phenomena. Here, in particular, we focus on the comparison between graphene and other semiconducting materials, concluding that a minimum of flicker noise at the charge neutrality point can appear only in the presence of a symmetric electron-hole behavior, a condition characteristic of graphene, but which is not found in the other commonly used semiconductors.

result.paraphrase: Graphene is of special interest for sensor implementation, and the ultimate performance of devices built from it is often governed by its flicker-noise characteristics. Compared with most ordinary semiconductors, graphene shows an unusual dependence of flicker-noise power spectral density on charge-carrier density. In most materials, flicker noise follows the empirical Hooge law, with power spectral density inversely proportional to the number of free carriers; however, in bilayer graphene, and sometimes monolayer graphene, an apparently counterintuitive minimum in flicker noise at the charge neutrality point has been observed. We explain this sharp difference using a model that enforces both the mass action law and the neutrality condition on charge fluctuations arising from trapping and detrapping phenomena. In particular, we compare graphene with other semiconducting materials and conclude that a minimum of flicker noise at the charge neutrality point can occur only when electron and hole behavior is symmetric, a condition characteristic of graphene but absent in the other commonly used semiconductors.
